282.history: The old harbour of the west was the first town of Dia-thìr to see the strangers, when three ships lay off its cape in the first year and their people spent forty days on the dunes below it while the council decided what to do with them. Oighrig nic Leòid, its custodian, gave them water before any vote allowed it. The humans prayed in one of its sail-lofts in those first winters, and the strangers' fever went out from its quays into the country. For a hundred years coal came down to it from the hill and went out in the humans' hulls. In the last autumn of the age its custodians shut the harbour to every Company ship, and it was from its quay that Lionel Strake sailed, with three chests of harbour keys set at his feet. Its sail-lofts and rope-stores filled with the humans' trade for a generation, and its custodians kept their own roll of every ship that came in, beside the harbour master's. In the siege year it was the one western harbour that answered neither side's letters.
282.known_for: the first landing, and the last ship

19.history: The capital held the Council of Custodians through all the years of the strangers, and the council's roll is the spine of the age's record. Here Gormshuil nic Fhearchair and the priest Samuel Wren made the first lists of words across a table, with a cup and a loaf; here the treaty was read in one tongue and signed, and here the council sat without a high custodian for ten years. When Lionel Strake came the Residency locked the council hall and took its keys, and the custodians sat on the floor of Macha's temple for two years. In the spring of the hundred and forty-ninth year the townsfolk broke the locks with a coal-hammer, held the Company's bridge with overturned carts, and fed the city from a sharing-yard behind the hall through the siege that followed. Its bells were rehung in a new frame by Torcall the mason in the first years. Tormod mac Ailein, high custodian when the ships came, was buried in the town, and Artair mac Iain was seated after the chair had stood empty ten years.
19.known_for: the council roll, and the sharing-yard of the siege year

27.history: Ros dhomhain lies a short walk below the capital on the lake shore, and it grew in the age into a second town of sawn timber and dressed stone beside the first. Pike's trading post stood on its quay, the Residency on the rise above it, and the Mission's chapel below. The mark and its hundred pence were first paid across its counter, its dockers struck beside the humans' own dockers, and the inquiry into the flood at Muileann chrom sat in the Residency's panelled room. In the war the harbour quarter held itself apart from both sides for a year, until its own men burned the tithe books of the counting-house by night and opened the lower gates to the council's companies. The Residency was found stripped at the end of an t-Sultain, its letter-books left whole on the shelves. Its quays took the coal of the hill from the barges for more than a century, and its steelyard and counting-house scales weighed every load. The Mission's chaplains kept their register of the dead in the chapel below the Residency, and Hannah Webb's brother Daniel was shipped from its quay with the human dockers after the strike.
27.known_for: the counting-house fire and the letter-books

242.history: The field village on the far western shore sent out the boats that first met the three ships, under the steersman Lachlann Odhar, who sent word home and went on south to Cuan shean. Its people told the story of that morning longer than any roll kept it, and they fished the same waters under the Sea-Watcher through all the years the strangers held the coast. Gorta Baile chrom, the Great Hunger that began in the north-west in the ninety-fourth year, reached it in its second winter and emptied many of its houses, and in the drought years a decade after it was named among the ten districts of the drought country. The houses stand close to the sea-wall, and the steersman's boat was kept drawn up on the shingle under them for as long as anyone remembered whose it had been.
242.known_for: the boats that met the strangers

17.history: The river port of the north-east grew in the age from a fishing town into a city on the trade of the strangers. Its shipwrights learned to build in the humans' fashion for the Company's coasting trade, and its fishwives kept the old market on the steps where cloth was still bartered for fish long after the mark was law. In the war the townsfolk burned the Company's coal where it lay stacked on the quays, sooner than let it fuel one more ship like the one that shelled Seann Toll. Its barges run down the Abhainn ghorm to the sea, and in the years of the Levy its carpenters were among the men the Administration took for the building of the beacon towers.
17.known_for: its shipwrights, and the coal burned on its quays

64.history: Seann Warr on the capital's western shore boils salt from the brine springs in the reed marsh behind the town, and it was the first place on the island to sell to Pike's counter, in the third year of the strangers, putting up its price when it heard what he would pay. Its carters took the salt round the lake to the capital for a century on their own roads. In the siege year it sent grain to the hills and the capital every month, by carts that went the long way round to avoid Strake's patrols. The Company tried twice to buy the pans outright and was twice refused, the salt-boilers holding that brine rising from the ground was no more theirs to sell than the rain.
64.known_for: brine salt, and the grain trains of the siege
